panel.title: Quatre jours pour travailler
panel.text: Depuis un an, les trente salariés de Clic & Colis, une petite entreprise nantaise qui prépare des colis pour des boutiques en ligne, ne travaillent plus que quatre jours par semaine. … L'idée vient de la directrice, Sophie Guérin. « Nos employés étaient fatigués, beaucoup étaient souvent malades, et nous avions du mal à recruter », explique-t-elle.
panel.question: Sophie Guérin a voulu changer l'organisation du travail parce que…
options: ses employés étaient souvent fatigués et malades.

sections.heading: What the written tests ask, level by level
intro: The DELF (Diplôme d'études en langue française, A1 to B2) and the DALF (Diplôme approfondi de langue française, C1 and C2) are diplomas of the French Ministry of Education, made by France Éducation international. Each level is a separate exam, and the diploma is valid for life. Every level also has a speaking test, which Glossa's papers do not include.

The TCF (Test de connaissance du français) is made by France Éducation international too, but has no levels to choose from: one test places you on a level from A1 to C2. Glossa's papers follow the general version, the TCF tout public.
rows: DELF A1
Listening (about 20 minutes, 21 items), reading (30 minutes, 20 items) and writing: a form and a message of at least 40 words (30 minutes).
The same task types with about half the items: listening 10 minutes, reading 15 minutes. Writing at full length, 30 minutes.
DELF A2
Listening (25 minutes, 22 items), reading (30 minutes, 23 items) and two texts of at least 60 words each (45 minutes).
Listening 14 minutes and reading 17 minutes, with about half the items. Writing at full length, 45 minutes.
DELF B1
Listening (about 25 minutes, 20 items), reading (45 minutes) and one opinion text of at least 160 words (45 minutes).
Listening 13 minutes and reading 24 minutes, with about half the questions. Writing at full length, 45 minutes.
DELF B2
Listening (about 30 minutes, 20 items), reading (1 hour) and one argued text of at least 250 words (1 hour).
Listening 17 minutes and reading 33 minutes, with about half the questions. Writing at full length, 1 hour.
DALF C1
Listening (about 40 minutes, 17 items), one text of about 1,000 words with 12 items (50 minutes), and a synthesis of documents plus an argued essay (2 hours 30 minutes).
9 listening items in 21 minutes and 6 reading items on a full-length text in 25 minutes. Writing at full length, 2 hours 30 minutes.
DALF C2
Reading and writing: one structured text of at least 700 words from a dossier of about 2,000 words (3 hours 30 minutes). Listening and speaking are a separate, individual test.
The reading-and-writing test at full length, 3 hours 30 minutes. No listening-and-speaking test.
TCF tout public
Listening (25 minutes, 29 questions), language structures (15 minutes, 18 questions) and reading (45 minutes, 29 questions), plus optional writing (3 tasks, 60 minutes) and speaking.
Listening 13 minutes, language structures 8 minutes and reading 23 minutes, with about half the questions. Writing at full length, 60 minutes, in every paper.
sections.note: Based on France Éducation international's published exam descriptions and sample papers and the TCF candidate's manual, checked in October 2026. Check them for the current format.

sections.heading: How the exams are passed or scored
items: DELF A1 to DALF C1: four tests of 25 points each. You pass with at least 50 of the 100 points and at least 5 of 25 in each test, so a strong test can make up for a weaker one, but a test below 5 fails the exam.
DALF C2: two tests of 50 points each. You pass with at least 50 of the 100 points and at least 10 of 50 in each test.

TCF: there is no pass or fail. Each test places you on a level from A1 to C2, and whether that is enough depends on the level the university, employer or authority asks for. The certificate is valid for two years.

Residence and nationality: the TCF IRN, a separate version of the TCF for residence and French nationality, uses the same kinds of tasks with different parts and timings. The authority that handles your application decides which test and level it accepts and sets the other conditions.

sections.heading: Papers to practise on, and a course to learn from

items.title: Two papers for each exam
items.text: Fourteen papers in all: two each for DELF A1, A2, B1 and B2, DALF C1 and C2 and the TCF, with original texts and recordings on everyday and public life, from moving house to the four-day week.

items.title: Writing rated against the criteria
items.text: Your texts are rated by AI against the DELF, DALF or TCF criteria, with what to improve. It is an estimate, not an examiner's mark.

items.title: A full course behind the papers
items.text: 76 modules in eight tiers from A1 to C1, with the tenses, the subjunctive, the pronouns and the nominal style of formal writing explained directly, so a weak spot in a paper has a module to go back to.

items.title: Feedback that says why
items.text: Every answer in the course gets feedback with a reason and a link to the grammar rule. Every French word can be tapped for its forms, meaning and audio.

sections.heading: How the practice papers differ from the real exams
items: No grade, score or level is given. A paper shows your share of the points. It applies the DELF and DALF pass rule to the tests it has, but cannot tell you what you would score in the real exam, and a TCF paper is not converted into a score from 100 to 699 or a level.
Listening and reading are shorter, with about half the items and the time cut to match. The writing is full length.
There is no speaking test at any level, and no listening-and-speaking test at C2. Glossa cannot assess free speech the way examiners do.
The TCF papers are not adaptive or weighted. The questions get harder as you go, as in the real test, but every question counts the same.
Recordings can be replayed. In the real exams you hear each recording once or twice, depending on the task; listen that many times and then answer.
One voice per recording. In dialogues and interviews both speakers are read by one voice, with their names or roles.
Words can be tapped for their meaning, in English as well, while you practise. The DALF C2 allows a monolingual French dictionary, so use tapping there as you would that dictionary.

items.question: Is Glossa an official DELF or TCF preparation course?
items.answer: No. Glossa is not connected with France Éducation international or the French Ministry of Education. The papers follow their published exam descriptions, with original content.

items.question: Which exam should I practise for?
items.answer: The one the school, employer or authority asks for. The DELF and DALF are taken at one level you choose and are valid for life; the TCF places you on a level and its certificate is valid for two years.

items.question: What is free?
items.answer: The whole French course from A1 to C1, the grammar reference and word practice are free. The practice papers, conversation practice, stories and the other extras are part of Premium.

items.question: I speak Finnish or German. Is there a course for me?
items.answer: Yes. French for Finnish speakers and French for German speakers have the same DELF, DALF and TCF papers, with the instructions and explanations in Finnish or German.

closing.heading: Start with the course, practise with the papers.
closing.text: Sign in with Google, take the placement test if you already know some French, and open the first module or the practice papers.
